concepts.title: Names and introductions
concepts.explanation: Io means I. Sono is the I-form of essere (to be). Italian often omits io because the verb identifies the speaker. Use sono with your name or nationality. Ciao is informal; buongiorno is a polite greeting.
concepts.commonError: With io, use sono, not è.

concepts.title: People and essere
concepts.explanation: Tu means you (one familiar person); lui and lei mean he and she. Essere changes: io sono, tu sei, lui/lei è. Use the accent on è (is): e without the accent means and.
concepts.commonError: With tu, essere is sei.

concepts.title: Family and avere
concepts.explanation: Avere means to have: io ho, tu hai, lui/lei ha. The h is silent but required. Un is an indefinite article with a masculine noun; una is feminine. Learn un fratello and una sorella as phrases.
concepts.commonError: With io, avere is ho. The h is silent.

concepts.title: Numbers and age
concepts.explanation: Italian expresses age with avere: ho venti anni literally means I have twenty years. Learn venti (twenty) and trenta (thirty). Hai asks about your age when the voice rises; writing adds a question mark.
concepts.commonError: Use avere for a person’s age: Ho venti anni.

concepts.title: Home and definite articles
concepts.explanation: Il means the with many masculine singular nouns; la with feminine singular nouns. Before a vowel both may become l’. Here casa is feminine and libro is masculine. In una casa means in a house.
concepts.commonError: Libro is masculine: il libro.

concepts.title: Colors and agreement
concepts.explanation: Many adjectives change -o to -a with feminine nouns. A white book is un libro bianco; a white house is una casa bianca. Grande works with either gender. These adjectives normally follow the noun.
concepts.commonError: Casa is feminine, so bianco becomes bianca.

concepts.title: More than one
concepts.explanation: Common masculine nouns change -o to -i: libro → libri. Many feminine nouns change -a to -e: casa → case. The articles also change: il → i; la → le. Sono means are with plural subjects as well as am with io.
concepts.commonError: Plural libri needs plural bianchi.

concepts.title: Study and work
concepts.explanation: Regular -are verbs replace -are with -o for io and -i for tu. Studiare → studio, studi. Lavorare → lavoro, lavori. Ogni giorno means every day. No extra helping verb is needed for I am studying in this context.
concepts.commonError: With io, studiare becomes studio.

concepts.title: Saying no and asking
concepts.explanation: Put non immediately before the verb to negate it: non studio. Do not add an equivalent of English do. A statement can become a yes/no question with intonation and a question mark. Keep subject and verb agreement.

examples.meaning: I do not work at home.

concepts.commonError: The verb still agrees with io: non lavoro.

concepts.title: Food and -ere verbs
concepts.explanation: Regular -ere verbs commonly use -o for io and -i for tu: prendere → prendo, prendi. In a café, prendo un caffè can mean I will have a coffee. Keep the accents on caffè and tè. Acqua is feminine: un’acqua.
concepts.commonError: With io, prendere becomes prendo.

concepts.title: What belongs to whom
concepts.explanation: Possessives agree with the thing owned: il mio libro, la mia casa, i miei libri. The owner’s gender does not determine mio or mia. Ordinary nouns usually keep the article before the possessive.
concepts.commonError: Mia agrees with feminine casa.

concepts.title: Going places
concepts.explanation: Andare is irregular: io vado, tu vai. Use a with cities, and combine a + la as alla, a + il as al. Vado alla stazione means I am going to the station. A Roma has no article.

examples.meaning: I am going to the station.

concepts.commonError: A + la contracts to alla.

concepts.title: Modal verbs and requests
concepts.explanation: Potere means can or be able to: io posso, tu puoi. Follow it with an infinitive: posso prendere. Do not conjugate both verbs. Per favore means please. Vorrei is a useful fixed polite request meaning I would like.
concepts.commonError: After posso, use the infinitive prendere.

concepts.title: Morning routines
concepts.explanation: Reflexive verbs use a pronoun referring back to the subject. Alzarsi means to get up: io mi alzo, tu ti alzi. Mi and ti go before the finite verb. Alle sette means at seven o’clock; alle combines a + le.

examples.meaning: Do you get up at seven?

concepts.commonError: For your own routine with io, use mi alzo.

concepts.title: A first look at the past
concepts.explanation: The passato prossimo combines an auxiliary and a past participle. With mangiare, use avere: ho mangiato. Regular -are participles end in -ato. Ieri means yesterday. This lesson introduces only the I-form with avere.
concepts.commonError: With io, avere is ho: Io ho mangiato.

concepts.title: Tomorrow and future plans
concepts.explanation: Italian often uses the present with a future time expression: domani vado a Roma. Domani makes the time clear. This is a first way to express plans before learning the future tense. Keep the irregular forms vado and vai.

examples.meaning: Tomorrow I am going to Rome.
Are you studying at home tomorrow?

concepts.commonError: Io uses vado, even when the plan is for tomorrow.

concepts.title: Days and dates
concepts.explanation: Italian days and months are masculine and written lowercase: lunedì, maggio. Give the date with the number, di and the month: il tre maggio. Oggi, domani and ieri frame any plan.

examples.target: Il compleanno è il tre maggio.

concepts.commonError: Days of the week are lowercase in Italian: lunedì.

concepts.title: Telling the time
concepts.explanation: Ask the time with Che ore sono? Answer È l’una for one o’clock and Sono le plus the number otherwise: Sono le tre. Add e mezza for half past, e un quarto for quarter past and meno un quarto for quarter to.
concepts.commonError: Hours take sono; only one o’clock takes è: Sono le tre.

concepts.title: Weather and seasons
concepts.explanation: Describe the weather with fa plus an adjective: fa caldo for hot, fa freddo for cold. Say c’è il sole for sunny and piove for it rains. Two seasons to know now are l’estate (summer) and l’inverno (winter).
concepts.commonError: Weather uses fare, not essere: Oggi fa freddo.

concepts.title: Market prices
concepts.explanation: Ask the price with Quanto costa? for one thing and Quanto costano? for several: Quanto costa un chilo di mele? Answer with the price: Tre euro. Un chilo is one kilo and il mercato is the market.

examples.target: Quanto costa un chilo di mele?
examples.meaning: How much is a kilo of apples?

concepts.commonError: Un chilo is singular, so the question is singular: Quanto costa un chilo di mele?

concepts.title: Saying where it hurts
concepts.explanation: Say pain with mi fa male plus the body part: Mi fa male la testa. Headache is il mal di testa and fever is la febbre. Answer Dove fa male? (Where does it hurt?) with Mi fa male plus the spot.
concepts.commonError: Pain uses fare, not essere: Mi fa male la testa.

concepts.title: Asking for medicine
concepts.explanation: Ask for medicine with Ho bisogno di…: Ho bisogno di una medicina. Una pastiglia is a pill and lo sciroppo is syrup. Ask the price with Quanto costa?: Costa cinque euro.
concepts.commonError: Bisogno needs di before the noun: Ho bisogno di una medicina.

concepts.title: Calling for help
concepts.explanation: Call for help with Aiuto! Ask for an ambulance with Chiami un’ambulanza! The emergency number is il centododici (112). Say È urgente when it is urgent.
concepts.commonError: Chiami is the polite command form: Chiami un’ambulanza!

concepts.title: Inviting and replying
concepts.explanation: Invite with Vuoi venire…?: Vuoi venire a cena? Accept with Sì, grazie, volentieri. Decline politely with Mi dispiace, non posso.

examples.meaning: Do you want to come to dinner Saturday?

concepts.commonError: Venire means to come: Vuoi venire a cena?

concepts.title: First words and greetings
concepts.explanation: Italian grew where Latin was spoken, and thousands of everyday words came into both Italian and English from Latin — nazione, informazione, ristorante, caffè. You can already recognize them before you speak a word of Italian. The words below are the first ones to say out loud: ciao greets friends a dozen times a day, grazie answers kindness, sì and no steer it.
concepts.commonError: Say ciao or buongiorno the moment you arrive — Italians notice warmth more than accent. Ciao is for friends and informal moments; buongiorno opens everything else.

activities.body: You already know hundreds of Italian words: nazione, informazione, ristorante.
